svg.text: Eight Things the Data Sheet Does Not Show
Two machines can carry the same throw distance and the same droplet size, stand in the same yard, and behave
nothing alike after a year of work. These eight are the least visible on a spec sheet, and the most influential on site.
Droplet size: nothing you can measure on site
Droplet size decides capture efficiency, and no instrument on site can measure it.
Nozzle wear, scaling and clogging filters coarsen the spray over months, not weeks.
→ Look at the design: anti-clog construction, water quality, pump curve margin.
Noise and vibration: only time will tell
On a test run the difference is hard to hear. Impeller balance and foundation
stiffness only show up over months of duty, usually with higher energy use.
→ Look at the design: fan and foundation, damping, what the daily check covers.
Throw distance: a design figure, not a tested one
Nameplate reach is theoretical: still air, no obstruction, one droplet size.
No mandatory test standard exists; the reference is the industry standard.
→ Fenghua is the first drafting unit of JB/T 13562-2018. Ask how it was measured.
Energy: a bigger motor is not a better machine
Reach comes from air volume, static pressure and droplet spectrum together,
not from motor power. At the same reach, extra power is electricity and noise.
→ Size the fan to the reach and coverage needed, with modest margin.
Level of automation: "automatic" means different things
A manual button, a remote control, a program (timer or zone) — and only
beyond that, interlocking with operations and adjustment on the result.
→ Ask what it does: per-zone start/stop, interlock with belts and trucks, records.
Durability: the plant is not asking for free repairs
What a plant wants is a machine that never needs repairing. The same model
fares very differently between sites, largely because of how it is maintained.
→ Ask about service access, consumable change-out, a documented schedule.
Design stability: the precondition for a long life
A settled model, a configuration that does not change every year, and parts
available for a decade are what let a plant build a maintenance routine.
→ An established manufacturer has an advantage: a platform that rarely changes.
Parameters and promises: "compliant" is not "achieved"
Many parameters cannot be verified on site, and they will not all be checked
item by item at delivery. Some promises made at tender are not met in service.
→ A long record, references that answer, and parts still available beat a spec sheet.
Clear answers to these eight are worth more than comparing throw and power on a nameplate.
